sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
August 2026 marked the fifth consecutive monthly advance for global equities, with major indices posting solid gains against a backdrop of extraordinary Q2 earnings results and persistent geopolitical tension stemming from the ongoing US-Iran conflict. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq led developed markets, fuelled by a technology earnings supercycle in which AI-exposed names delivered outsized profit growth far exceeding analyst expectations.

Divergence defined the global tape: Germany's DAX struck fresh all-time highs, European commodity-linked names benefited from surging energy prices, and Japan's Nikkei 225 remained well-supported by a weak-yen tailwind. Chinese equities bifurcated by exchange — mainland Shanghai edging modestly higher on domestic stimulus measures while Hong Kong's Hang Seng lagged, pressured by global growth uncertainty and elevated energy import costs tied to the Hormuz supply disruption.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes: Iran War / Strait of Hormuz Crisis -- The enduring market overhang of the 2026 US-Iran conflict intensified in August, with Iranian officials escalating rhetoric around the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil and gas historically transited before the war. Brent crude surged to an intra-month high of approximately **$95/bbl** before easing to **$90.80/bbl** by month-end, logging a monthly advance of **+8.39%** that reverberated across energy equities and inflation expectations globally. On the final trading day of August, fresh US military strikes on Iranian positions triggered a sharp single-session selloff — the Dow surrendering **374 points** — though the broader monthly tape remained firmly positive. The geopolitical risk premium embedded in oil is now a persistent structural feature of the 2026 macro landscape, complicating central bank rate paths and squeezing energy-import-dependent economies across Europe and APAC.

AI Mega-Earnings Supercycle -- Exceptional Q2 2026 corporate earnings provided the fundamental backbone for equity strength in August, with S&P 500 blended year-over-year EPS growth clocking in at approximately **+50.4%** — the highest quarterly growth rate in recent memory. The technology sector was the epicentre, posting a **+74%** profit surge as Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, and others monetised AI infrastructure investments at scale; Alphabet and Amazon specifically recognised large mark-to-market gains on stakes in Anthropic and other AI highfliers. Of the 88% of S&P 500 companies that had reported by early August, 86% beat consensus estimates, and sell-side analysts project CY2026 full-year EPS growth of approximately **+30%**, sustaining the forward momentum. The Nasdaq's monthly gain of approximately **+4%** reflects the capital concentration into mega-cap technology that the AI investment thesis continues to drive, now validated by reported financials rather than narrative alone.

Gold's Record-Breaking Safe-Haven Surge -- Gold was the commodity standout of August, surging **+8.51%** for the month to close at **$4,431/oz** from a monthly open near **$4,083/oz** — an extraordinary single-month advance reflecting the convergence of geopolitical safe-haven demand, a broadly range-bound dollar, and accelerating central bank accumulation. The metal benefited from the dual tailwind of the Iran war's oil supply shock (which eroded confidence in Middle Eastern-linked risk assets) and investor uncertainty over the inflation implications of surging energy prices for developed-market monetary policy, which simultaneously argues against near-term rate cuts and reduces the opportunity cost of holding gold. Institutional positioning in gold-backed ETFs has risen materially through 2026, and the metal now trades well above prior all-time highs set in 2025, cementing its status as the preeminent macro hedge of the current cycle.

Bank of Japan Normalisation and Yen Volatility -- The Bank of Japan's trajectory toward policy normalisation was a dominant APAC macro theme in August, with the central bank's own policy summary explicitly flagging upside inflation risks and a potentially faster-than-expected rate-hike path. Markets priced in the near-certain probability of a **25bp** hike at the September meeting — which subsequently materialised, taking the BOJ policy rate to **1.25%**, the highest level since 1995. A weakening yen, with USD/JPY trading near **157** (approx., verify before merging) at various points in August, paradoxically supported Japan's export-oriented corporates and kept the Nikkei 225 well-bid, as cheaper currency directly boosted yen-denominated repatriated earnings. The BOJ normalisation story is the most consequential cross-asset variable for APAC portfolio managers, given the yen's central role in funding global carry trades and its knock-on effects on JGB yields and Japanese institutional investor hedging flows.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equity markets delivered another constructive month in August, with the S&P 500 gaining approximately **+2.7%** to close at **7,686.14** and the Nasdaq Composite advancing roughly **+4%** to **26,370.89** — both indices marking their fifth consecutive monthly gain. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added approximately **+1%** to close at **53,185.90**, though a sharp late-month reversal on August 31 — driven by fresh US strikes on Iranian military positions — saw the Dow surrender **374 points** on the final session alone, illustrating the geopolitical volatility embedded in the current tape.

The fundamental driver was a blowout Q2 2026 earnings season: of S&P 500 companies reporting by early August, 86% exceeded consensus estimates, with blended year-over-year EPS growth of approximately **+50.4%**. The technology sector was the primary engine, with profits up **+74%** year-over-year as AI infrastructure monetisation gathered pace across mega-cap names. Nvidia rallied following strong revenue guidance issued on August 26, while Alphabet and Amazon recognised large gains from AI equity stakes, juicing reported profits well above underlying operating income.

A tame July CPI print released in mid-August provided an additional tailwind, reinforcing the disinflation narrative in core goods and services even as rising oil prices threaten to reintroduce headline inflation pressure. The Fed's policy path is now more nuanced: the disinflationary impulse from goods and services argues for eventual rate relief, but an energy supply shock complicates the timing — and markets spent much of August recalibrating rate-cut timing further into 2027.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities delivered a divergent performance in August, with Germany's DAX leading the continent by closing at a fresh all-time high of **26,569.99** on August 28, underpinned by a resilient corporate earnings cycle and continued recovery momentum in German industrial output. The FTSE 100 traded in the region of **10,800** (approx., verify before merging), benefiting from its heavy energy and mining sector weighting as Brent crude surged **+8.39%** for the month; the CAC 40 underperformed continental peers, dragged by consumer discretionary weakness and rising energy import costs (approx. monthly return, verify before merging).

The ECB held no scheduled meeting in August, but the lingering effect of its June decision — a **25bp** rate hike that took the deposit facility rate to **2.25%** — continued to push eurozone sovereign yields higher. Peripheral spreads, particularly Italian BTPs versus German Bunds, widened modestly as markets revised their ECB easing timelines further out in response to oil-driven inflation re-acceleration, keeping the risk premium on higher-debt sovereigns elevated.

Europe sits at an uncomfortable macro intersection: energy-intensive industries face a stagflationary squeeze from the Hormuz-driven oil and gas price surge, while the ECB must balance external commodity inflation against slowing domestic demand. The DAX's outperformance reflects Germany's export and industrial resilience, but the broader eurozone growth outlook is increasingly clouded by the twin headwinds of elevated energy costs and tighter financing conditions.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Japan's Nikkei 225 was broadly supported through August, trading in the approximate **66,400–68,700** range (approx., verify before merging) as a persistently weak yen provided an ongoing tailwind for the country's export-oriented corporates. The Bank of Japan's increasingly explicit hawkish posture — flagging upside inflation risks and a potentially accelerated normalisation path — paradoxically underpinned equities, as investors interpreted the signal as an expression of genuine economic and wage growth strength rather than a harbinger of destabilising tightening.

China's equity markets diverged by exchange: the Shanghai Composite edged modestly higher on the back of targeted domestic stimulus measures and signs of stabilising manufacturing activity (approx. monthly return, verify before merging). Hong Kong's Hang Seng, by contrast, underperformed as investors weighed the implications of slowing global demand, elevated energy import costs, and ongoing uncertainty about China's property sector recovery for Hong Kong-listed names — which carry greater sensitivity to foreign capital flows than the domestically dominated A-share market (approx. monthly return, verify before merging).

Across the APAC region in August, markets navigated two competing forces: the geopolitical oil supply shock, which meaningfully increases energy import bills for Japan, Korea, and China, and the structural AI hardware demand rotation, which boosted Taiwanese semiconductor names and benefited from the global tech capex super-cycle anchored in the US.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US Dollar Index (DXY) was broadly range-bound in August, beginning the month near **99.78**, averaging approximately **100.12** across the period, and settling near **100.23** — a marginal monthly gain of roughly **+0.5%**, with an intra-month range of **98.73–101.73**. Competing forces largely offset one another: geopolitical safe-haven demand for the dollar (from renewed Iran conflict escalation) was countered by a tame US inflation print in mid-August and by market reassessment of the dollar's structural role in a world where US fiscal risks and the Hormuz supply shock are ongoing overhangs.

EUR/USD traded near **1.1593** in mid-August (approx. end-of-month close, verify before merging), with the pair facing modest headwinds as the ECB's tightening cycle appeared to be nearing its terminal rate, reducing forward rate-differential support for the euro. GBP/USD held near **1.3559** mid-month (approx. end-of-month close, verify before merging), broadly stable as the Bank of England maintained its data-dependent posture. USD/JPY remained elevated near **157** (approx., verify before merging), as the yen faced persistent carry-trade selling despite the BOJ's hawkish signalling — the rate differential versus the US still overwhelmingly favoured yen-funded carry strategies.

The structural backdrop in FX remains a gradual unwinding of the peak-dollar thesis: the DXY has trended lower from its 2024–2025 highs as US growth exceptionalism fades at the margins. However, the 2026 oil supply shock has introduced a new, less predictable source of dollar support via petrodollar recycling and safe-haven demand, complicating the bear-dollar consensus that entered the year with significant conviction.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
August 2026 was an exceptional month for commodities, with energy and precious metals the standout performers. Brent crude surged **+8.39%** to settle at **$90.80/bbl** on August 31, after touching an intra-month high of approximately **$95/bbl** as Strait of Hormuz disruptions intensified and Iranian officials escalated rhetoric over potential offensive action in the waterway. WTI crude made comparable gains (approx. end-of-month close and monthly %, verify before merging), with US benchmark crude up approximately **+33%** year-over-year — underscoring the cumulative price impact of the 2026 oil supply shock that began with the February US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

Gold was the month's standout performer, advancing **+8.51%** from an August open of **$4,083/oz** to close at **$4,431/oz** — a record monthly settlement. The advance was driven by the convergence of Middle East safe-haven demand, a broadly stable-to-soft dollar, and accelerating central bank gold purchases that have been a structural feature of markets since 2023. Copper continued its record-breaking run, trading near **$6.35/lb** on COMEX (approx., verify before merging), sustained by structural demand from AI data centre build-out and global energy transition infrastructure investment against a backdrop of constrained mine supply growth.

The oil supply shock carries cascading effects across the commodity complex: elevated energy input costs are feeding through to fertilisers, petrochemicals, and container shipping rates, creating broad-based inflationary pressure that is structurally distinct from prior demand-driven commodity cycles and considerably harder for central banks to address via interest rate policy alone.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
US Treasury yields drifted higher through August in a bear-flattening pattern, with the 10-year yield ending the month at approximately **4.73%** and the 2-year yield closing near **4.34%** — up from earlier-month readings of **4.68%** and **4.17%** respectively. The 10-year/2-year spread narrowed from approximately **51bps** to roughly **39bps** over the course of August, reflecting the short end's greater sensitivity to the revised-later Fed rate-cut timeline as the energy-driven inflation impulse complicated the clean disinflationary narrative.

The bear-flattening dynamic is consistent with markets pricing a higher-for-longer Fed hold in the near term while retaining the expectation of eventual easing once the commodity supply shock's inflationary impact dissipates. Notably, the 10-year yield continued its ascent into September, approaching **5%** — suggesting August's elevated levels were a staging post rather than a ceiling, and that the term premium for duration risk remains inadequate given the fiscal and inflation uncertainties in the current environment.

Eurozone government bonds remained under pressure following the ECB's June tightening: the absence of an August ECB meeting provided no catalyst for relief, and oil-sensitive inflation data kept the probability of near-term ECB rate cuts depressed. Globally, fixed income markets are navigating a nuanced intersection of genuine goods and services disinflation and a commodity supply shock that reintroduces upside headline inflation risk — a combination that argues for duration caution and favours short-to-intermediate maturities over the long end.
